tips: Follow the argument in order. Paul builds step by step: all have sinned (chapters 1–3), justification by faith (3–5), new life in the Spirit (6–8), Israel in God's plan (9–11), and life together in the church (12–16).
Watch for Paul's questions, such as "What shall we say then?" (Romans 6:1). He anticipates objections and answers them, so read each question as a turn in the argument.
Notice the word "therefore" at Romans 12:1. The practical instructions of chapters 12–16 rest on "the mercies of God" described in chapters 1–11.

looksBack.title: Abraham's faith
looksBack.text: Paul's key example is Abraham, whose faith "was counted unto him for righteousness" (Romans 4:3; Genesis 15:6).

looksBack.title: Adam and Christ
looksBack.text: Paul contrasts Adam's disobedience, which brought death (Genesis 3), with Christ's obedience, which brings life (Romans 5:12–21).

looksAhead.title: Galatians
looksAhead.text: Galatians argues many of the same points in a sharper, more urgent tone, including justification by faith and Abraham's example (Galatians 2:16; 3:6–9).

looksAhead.title: Paul's journey to Rome
looksAhead.text: Paul hoped to visit Rome on his way to Spain (Romans 15:23–24); he arrived years later as a prisoner (Acts 28:14–16).

tips: Read it as Paul's answers to a troubled church. Chapters 1–6 respond to reports he has heard; from chapter 7 on he answers questions they wrote to him, often introduced with "Now concerning…" (1 Corinthians 7:1; 8:1; 12:1).
Keep the city in mind. Corinth was a wealthy, proud, and morally loose port city, and many of the church's problems—divisions, lawsuits, sexual immorality—came from its culture.
Read the famous love chapter (chapter 13) in context. It is placed in the middle of Paul's correction about spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14), where love was missing.

looksBack.title: The founding of the church
looksBack.text: Paul founded the church in Corinth during an eighteen-month stay (Acts 18:1–11).

looksAhead.title: A painful relationship
looksAhead.text: 2 Corinthians continues the story, revealing a painful visit and a tearful letter after this one (2 Corinthians 2:1–4).

looksAhead.title: The resurrection body
looksAhead.text: Paul's teaching on the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15) is the Bible's fullest discussion of the subject and connects to the hope of Christ's return in 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18.

tips: Read it as Paul's most personal letter. He defends his ministry against critics and opens his heart about weakness, suffering, and his love for the church.
Notice the paradox at the center of the letter: God's power is shown through human weakness. "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9).
Expect sudden changes in tone. Chapters 1–7 are warm and relieved, chapters 8–9 are about a collection for Jerusalem, and chapters 10–13 are sharp and defensive.

looksBack.title: After 1 Corinthians
looksBack.text: Paul mentions a painful visit and a letter written "with many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:1–4) that came after 1 Corinthians.

looksBack.title: Moses' veil
looksBack.text: Paul contrasts the old covenant with the new by recalling the veil Moses wore over his shining face (2 Corinthians 3:7–18; Exodus 34:29–35).

looksAhead.title: The collection for Jerusalem
looksAhead.text: The gift Paul urges in chapters 8–9 is delivered when he goes to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; Acts 24:17).

tips: Notice what is missing from the opening: Paul gives no thanksgiving for the readers. He goes straight to his astonishment that they are turning to "another gospel" (Galatians 1:6).

Understand the conflict. Teachers were telling Gentile believers they had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God's people; Paul insists they are justified by faith in Christ alone (Galatians 2:16).

Read chapters 5–6 as the answer to the question of how believers should then live. Freedom in Christ is not license but life by the Spirit, which produces "the fruit of the Spirit" (Galatians 5:22–23).

looksBack.title: Abraham and the promise
looksBack.text: Paul argues that the promise to Abraham came 430 years before the law (Galatians 3:17), so the law cannot cancel it (Genesis 15:6; 12:3).

looksBack.title: Paul's story
looksBack.text: Paul's account of his conversion and visits to Jerusalem (Galatians 1:13–2:10) can be compared with Acts 9 and Acts 15.

looksAhead.title: Romans
looksAhead.text: Romans develops the same gospel of justification by faith more fully and calmly (Romans 3:21–4:25).

tips: Notice the two halves. Chapters 1–3 describe what God has done in Christ; chapters 4–6 begin with "walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called" (Ephesians 4:1) and describe how to live in response.
Read the opening (Ephesians 1:3–14) slowly. In Greek it is one long sentence of praise for every spiritual blessing in Christ.
Watch for the theme of unity. Jews and Gentiles are made "one new man" in Christ (Ephesians 2:14–16), and the church is called to keep "the unity of the Spirit" (Ephesians 4:3).

looksBack.title: Paul in Ephesus
looksBack.text: Paul spent about three years in Ephesus (Acts 19:8–10; 20:31), and his farewell to the Ephesian elders is recorded in Acts 20:17–38.

looksAhead.title: Colossians
looksAhead.text: Ephesians and Colossians share many themes and phrases, including instructions for households (Ephesians 5:22–6:9; Colossians 3:18–4:1).

looksAhead.title: Christ's letter to Ephesus
looksAhead.text: Decades later, the risen Christ commends the church in Ephesus for its endurance but warns that it has left its first love (Revelation 2:1–7).

tips: Read it as a thank-you letter from prison. Paul thanks the Philippians for their gift and partnership, and the word "joy" or "rejoice" appears throughout (Philippians 4:4).
Notice the hymn about Christ in Philippians 2:5–11. Paul uses Christ's humility—emptying himself and becoming obedient to death—as the model for how believers should treat each other.
Watch for the practical problems behind the joy: a quarrel between two women in the church (Philippians 4:2) and a warning about those who insisted on circumcision (Philippians 3:2–3).

looksBack.title: A church founded in Acts
looksBack.text: The church in Philippi began with Lydia's household and a jailer who believed after an earthquake (Acts 16:12–34).

looksAhead.title: Every knee shall bow
looksAhead.text: Philippians 2:10–11 applies Isaiah 45:23 to Jesus; the scene of all creation worshiping is pictured in Revelation 5:13.

tips: Start with the great hymn to Christ (Colossians 1:15–20). The whole letter depends on its claim that Christ is above all things and that in him all fullness dwells.

Try to picture the false teaching Paul is answering: human philosophy, food laws and festivals, the worship of angels, and harsh treatment of the body (Colossians 2:8, 16–23). His answer is always Christ's sufficiency.
Notice how the letter turns practical in chapter 3. Because believers are "risen with Christ" (Colossians 3:1), they are to put off the old life and put on the new.

looksBack.title: Paul's work in Asia
looksBack.text: The church at Colossae likely began during Paul's long stay in Ephesus, when "all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word" (Acts 19:10).

looksAhead.title: Philemon
looksAhead.text: Onesimus, mentioned in Colossians 4:9, is the runaway slave at the center of Paul's letter to Philemon, carried at the same time.

looksAhead.title: The letter from Laodicea
looksAhead.text: Paul asks that this letter be shared with the church at Laodicea (Colossians 4:16), a church later addressed in Revelation 3:14–22.

tips: Read it as a letter to new believers. Paul had been with them only a short time, and he writes to encourage them in persecution and fill in gaps in their teaching.
Notice that each chapter ends with a mention of Christ's coming (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 2:19; 3:13; 4:17; 5:23). Hope in his return shapes the whole letter.
Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 with its purpose in mind. Paul is comforting grieving believers who feared that those who had died would miss Christ's return.

looksBack.title: A hasty departure
looksBack.text: Paul preached in Thessalonica for a short time before opposition forced him to leave by night (Acts 17:1–10).

looksAhead.title: 2 Thessalonians
looksAhead.text: Confusion about the day of the Lord led Paul to write again soon after (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3).

looksAhead.title: The resurrection
looksAhead.text: The hope that the dead in Christ will rise is explained further in 1 Corinthians 15:51–57.

tips: Read it right after 1 Thessalonians. It corrects a misunderstanding—some believed the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2).
Approach chapter 2 with care. Paul refers to things he had already taught the church in person (2 Thessalonians 2:5), so some details about "that man of sin" are hard to interpret today.
Notice the practical problem in chapter 3. Some believers had stopped working, perhaps expecting the end; Paul answers, "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

looksBack.title: Continuing 1 Thessalonians
looksBack.text: The letter builds on Paul's earlier teaching about Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:11).

looksBack.title: Daniel's visions
looksBack.text: The description of one who exalts himself above every god (2 Thessalonians 2:4) recalls Daniel 11:36.

looksAhead.title: The final victory
looksAhead.text: The Lord's defeat of the lawless one "with the spirit of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8) is echoed in Revelation 19:15, 20.

tips: Read it as instructions to a young leader. Timothy had been left in Ephesus to correct false teachers and bring order to the church (1 Timothy 1:3–4).
Notice the purpose statement in 1 Timothy 3:14–15: Paul writes so that Timothy will know how people ought to behave in the house of God, "the pillar and ground of the truth."
Watch for the short statements of faith, such as "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners" (1 Timothy 1:15). These faithful sayings were likely familiar summaries in the early church.

looksBack.title: Timothy's story
looksBack.text: Timothy joined Paul on his second missionary journey (Acts 16:1–3); his mother and grandmother taught him the scriptures (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15).

looksAhead.title: Paul's last letter
looksAhead.text: 2 Timothy, written later from prison, is Paul's final charge to the same young leader.

looksAhead.title: Leaders in Crete
looksAhead.text: Titus gives similar qualifications for church leaders (Titus 1:5–9; 1 Timothy 3:1–13).

tips: Read it as a farewell. Paul is in prison, many have deserted him, and he knows his death is near (2 Timothy 4:6–8). These are his last words to his closest coworker.
Notice the repeated call to endure: "be not thou therefore ashamed" (2 Timothy 1:8) and "endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2 Timothy 2:3).
Pay attention to what Paul says about scripture: it is "given by inspiration of God" and able to make one "wise unto salvation" (2 Timothy 3:15–16).

looksBack.title: 1 Timothy
looksBack.text: Timothy is still facing the false teaching Paul warned about earlier (1 Timothy 1:3–7; 2 Timothy 2:16–18).

looksAhead.title: Mark is useful again
looksAhead.text: Paul asks for Mark, "for he is profitable to me for the ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11), a reconciliation after their earlier parting (Acts 15:37–39).

looksAhead.title: The crown of righteousness
looksAhead.text: Paul's confidence in "a crown of righteousness" (2 Timothy 4:8) echoes the promises of crowns for the faithful in James 1:12 and Revelation 2:10.

tips: Read it as a short handbook for a new church. Titus is to appoint elders in every city of Crete and teach sound doctrine (Titus 1:5).
Notice the repeated link between belief and behavior. The phrase "good works" appears again and again (Titus 2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14)—not as a way to be saved, but as the result of God's grace.
Read the two great summaries of the gospel (Titus 2:11–14; 3:4–7). They explain why Christians should live differently.

looksBack.title: Who was Titus?
looksBack.text: Titus was a Gentile coworker of Paul who went with him to Jerusalem (Galatians 2:1–3) and was sent to Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6–7; 8:16–17).

looksAhead.title: The blessed hope
looksAhead.text: Paul's description of waiting for "that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing" of Christ (Titus 2:13) connects to the vision of his return in Revelation 19:11–16.

tips: Learn the situation first. Onesimus, a slave who had run away from his master Philemon, became a believer through Paul, and Paul is sending him back with this letter.

Watch how Paul persuades rather than commands (Philemon 1:8–9). He appeals to love, offers to pay any debt himself (Philemon 1:18–19), and asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as "a brother beloved" (Philemon 1:16).
Notice the wordplay. Onesimus means "useful," and Paul says he was once unprofitable but is now profitable (Philemon 1:11).

looksBack.title: Sent with Colossians
looksBack.text: Onesimus travels with Tychicus, who carried the letter to the Colossians (Colossians 4:7–9).

looksAhead.title: Neither bond nor free
looksAhead.text: The letter puts into practice Paul's teaching that in Christ "there is neither bond nor free" (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11).
